title: Stock Exchange Matching Engine
prompt: Design the core of a stock exchange: brokers send buy and sell orders, the exchange matches them into trades, and everyone gets a live view of the order book. Fairness and speed both matter.

clarify.q: Who connects: retail users directly, or only member brokers?
clarify.why: Brokers on dedicated lines and a binary protocol make microsecond latency realistic. Retail over the internet would need a web tier and changes the latency target by three orders of magnitude.

clarify.q: Which order types: limit and market only, or also stop, iceberg, IOC and FOK?
clarify.why: Limit, market, cancel and replace define the core data structure. Each extra type adds rules inside the matching loop, which is the most latency-sensitive code.

clarify.q: How many symbols, and how skewed is traffic across them?
clarify.why: A few hot symbols decide whether one core per symbol is enough. Partitioning is by symbol, so skew sets the size of the biggest partition.

clarify.q: What latency target, and is it the median or the tail?
clarify.why: A p99 of about 100 µs inside the exchange rules out disks in the hot path, garbage-collected heaps without care, and cross-datacenter hops.

clarify.q: Is there a continuous session only, or also opening and closing auctions?
clarify.why: Auctions collect orders and match them at one price. That is a different algorithm and a burst of load at the open and close.

clarify.q: Are clearing, settlement and the broker's own risk systems in scope?
clarify.why: Usually no. Saying so keeps the design on the matching path. We still need light pre-trade risk checks at the gateway.

clarify.q: What must happen if the matching engine host dies?
clarify.why: Regulators expect no lost acknowledged orders and a short halt at most. That drives the sequencer, the journal and the hot standby design.

functional: Brokers place limit and market orders, cancel them, and replace (change price or quantity).
Orders match by price-time priority: best price first, then earliest arrival at that price.
Brokers receive an execution report for every accept, fill, partial fill, cancel and reject.
Publish market data: trades, top of book, and full depth per symbol.
Pre-trade risk checks reject orders that break a broker's limits.
nonFunctional: Order-in to ack-out inside the exchange: median under 50 µs, p99 under 100 µs.
Deterministic: replaying the same input sequence produces exactly the same trades and book.
No acknowledged order is lost. Failover to a standby in under 1 s.
Fairness: the same arrival order for everyone, market data sent to all subscribers at the same moment.
Sustain 1 M order messages/s at the opening burst.
outOfScope: Broker apps and retail trading UIs.
Regulatory reporting formats (we keep the data they need).
Opening and closing auction algorithm details.

assumptions: 5 000 symbols, trading session of 6.5 hours (23 400 s)
2 B order messages per day (new, cancel, replace), cancels dominate
Opening and closing bursts reach 10× the average rate
The hottest symbol takes about 5% of all messages
Binary message ≈ 100 bytes. 50 M trades per day
Average 10 k resting orders per symbol

steps.label: Hottest symbol at peak
steps.math: 1 M/s × 5% = 50 k/s. Matching costs ≈ 2 µs per message → one core does ≈ 500 k/s
steps.result: ≈ 10% of one core. One thread per symbol is plenty.

steps.label: Journal size
steps.result: ≈ 200 GB/day. Peak write rate 1 M/s × 100 B = 100 MB/s, sequential

steps.label: Order book memory
steps.result: ≈ 5 GB, about 15 GB with indexes. Fits in RAM.

steps.label: Market data bandwidth
steps.math: 1 M events/s × 100 B = 100 MB/s = 800 Mbps. To 1 000 subscribers by unicast: 800 Gbps
steps.result: Unicast is impossible at peak. Use multicast: send each packet once.

steps.label: Latency budget
steps.math: gateway parse + risk 10 + hop 5 + sequence and replicate 20 + hop 5 + match 5 + hop 5 + encode and send 5 (µs)
steps.result: ≈ 55 µs median, leaving headroom under the 100 µs p99 target

estimates.takeaway: Throughput is not the hard part: even the hottest symbol uses a fraction of one core, and the whole book fits in RAM. The hard parts are tail latency (no disk, no locks, no GC pauses on the hot path), determinism (so a standby can take over with an identical book), and fan-out of market data, which only works with multicast at 800 Mbps of raw feed.

api.body: { clOrdId, symbol, side, type: LIMIT|MARKET, price?, qty, tif: DAY|IOC }
api.note: clOrdId is unique per broker session, so a resend after reconnect is detected and not double-booked.
Cancel can race a fill. Whatever the sequencer orders first wins.
Price change or quantity increase loses time priority. Quantity decrease keeps it.

api.returns: { orderId, status: PARTIAL|FILLED, lastQty, lastPx, leavesQty, tradeId, seq }
api.note: Sent to both sides of each trade over their order sessions.

api.path: Market data feed, one group per symbol range
api.returns: { seq, symbol, type: ADD|CANCEL|EXEC|TRADE, price, qty, orderRef }
api.note: Per-channel sequence numbers. Gaps are filled from a retransmit service or a snapshot channel.
Delayed or conflated view for web consumers, served from a downstream cache, never the engine.

entities.name: Order (in memory)
entities.store: Matching engine RAM, rebuilt from the journal
fields: arrival order, the time in price-time
position in the price level FIFO
entities.why: Lives only in memory on the hot path. The journal is the durable copy.

entities.name: Journal entry
entities.store: Append-only file on local NVMe, replicated to standby and archive
fields: stamped by the sequencer, not the engine
entities.why: The single input history. Replay it through the engine and you get the same book and trades.

entities.name: Trade
entities.store: Emitted as output events, stored downstream in a columnar store
entities.why: Consumed by clearing, surveillance and market data. Never read back by the engine.

entities.name: Risk limits
entities.store: Gateway memory, loaded from a risk DB at start of day
entities.why: Checked before an order enters the sequencer, so bad orders never touch the book.

data.note: The design is event sourced at its core: the journal of sequenced inputs is the truth; the book is a pure function of it. Prices are integers in ticks (a price of 100.15 with a 0.01 tick is 10 015). Outputs (exec reports, trades, market data) are also stamped with the input seq that produced them, so any consumer can line them up exactly. Downstream stores (trades for clearing, history for surveillance) are fed asynchronously and are off the latency path.

hld.summary:
Brokers connect to order gateways that parse the binary protocol, authenticate the session, and run pre-trade risk checks. Valid orders go to the sequencer for their symbol partition, which stamps a gap-free sequence number and timestamp, writes the message to the journal, and makes sure the hot standby has it before passing it on. The matching engine is a single thread per partition that applies inputs in sequence order to in-memory order books and emits fills and book changes.

Outputs go two ways: exec reports back through the gateway to the brokers involved, and book events to the market data publisher, which builds depth and top-of-book feeds and multicasts them. A standby engine consumes the same sequenced stream and holds an identical book, ready to take over. Everything slow (trade storage, clearing, surveillance, web views) hangs off the output stream asynchronously.

diagram.title: Order path and market data
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  BR[Broker sessions] --> GW[Order gateways with risk checks]
  GW --> SEQ[Sequencer per partition]
  SEQ --> JR[(Journal)]
  SEQ --> ME[Matching engine primary]
  SEQ --> SB[Standby engine]
  ME --> GW
  ME --> MD[Market data publisher]
  MD --> MC[Multicast feeds]
  MD --> RT[Retransmit and snapshot service]
  ME --> DS[Downstream trade store and clearing]
  MC --> SUB[Subscribers]

flows.title: A limit order that partly fills
steps: Gateway receives BUY 400 @ 100.15, checks the broker's limits, forwards it.
Sequencer stamps seq 9 001 and journals it. Standby confirms receipt.
Engine walks the ask side from the best price: fills 300 against order 1 and 100 against order 2, both at 100.10 (the resting price). 300 + 100 = 400, so the buy is done; order 2 keeps 100.
Engine emits two trades, exec reports to three orders, and book events. The buyer gets price improvement of 0.05 per share.

flows.title: Cancel racing a fill
steps: Seller sends cancel for order 2 while the buy above is in flight.
Both messages reach the sequencer. Whichever gets the lower seq is applied first.
If the buy was first, the cancel only removes the remaining 100 and reports that 100 was already filled.

flows.title: Engine host fails
steps: Heartbeats from the primary stop. A failover controller with a lease promotes the standby.
Standby has applied every sequenced message up to the last one the sequencer journaled, so its book is identical.
Gateways and the market data publisher switch to the new primary and resume from the next seq. Downstream consumers dedupe by seq.

deepDives.title: The order book data structure
deepDives.problem: Every message needs to find the best price, walk price levels in order, append to the back of a level, and remove any order by id (cancels are most of the traffic). All of that must take microseconds, with no allocation on the hot path.

options.name: Sorted tree of price levels, FIFO list per level, hash map by order id
options.how: Each side is a balanced tree (or skip list) keyed by price. Each level holds a doubly linked list of orders in arrival order. A hash map orderId → list node gives O(1) cancel. Cache a pointer to the best level.
pros: Handles any price range
Cancel and add at an existing level are O(1); new level is O(log L)
cons: Tree nodes scattered in memory, cache misses
Rebalancing costs on level create and delete

options.name: Array indexed by price tick, plus FIFO lists and the id map
options.how: Pre-allocate an array covering a band around the reference price (for example ±20% in ticks). Index = price in ticks minus band floor. Track best bid and ask indexes.
pros: O(1) level lookup, cache friendly
No rebalancing, no allocation during trading
cons: Finding the next non-empty level after a level empties needs a scan or a bitmap
Prices outside the band need a fallback path or are rejected by price collars

options.name: Single sorted list of all orders
options.how: One list ordered by price then time.
pros: Simple
cons: Insert and cancel are O(n). Unusable at 10 k resting orders.

deepDives.choice: I would use the tick-indexed array with a bitmap of non-empty levels for each side, intrusive doubly linked FIFO lists, a pre-sized open-addressing hash map from orderId to node, and an object pool so nothing is allocated while trading. Price collars (reject orders far from the reference price) keep everything in the band, which is also a market-integrity rule. For instruments with huge or unbounded price ranges I'd fall back to the tree. Either way, price is an integer number of ticks; floats would make equal prices compare unequal.

deepDives.title: Single-threaded matching engine per symbol
deepDives.problem: Matching mutates shared state on every message: the book, order states, the trade id counter. Multiple threads on one book would need locks, and lock contention creates exactly the tail latency we are trying to avoid. Worse, two threads could let a later order match before an earlier one, which breaks fairness.

options.name: One thread owns a partition of symbols, pinned to a core
options.how: Partition symbols across engine threads. Each thread busy-polls its input ring buffer and processes messages one at a time. No locks; nothing else touches that memory.
pros: No locks, predictable latency
Order of processing equals sequence order, so fairness is built in
Deterministic, which makes replay possible
cons: A single symbol cannot use more than one core
Busy polling burns a core even when idle
A slow message (huge sweep) delays everything behind it in that partition

options.name: Thread pool with a lock per book
options.how: Any worker takes the symbol's lock, processes, releases.
pros: Uses all cores for any mix of symbols
cons: Lock handoff adds microseconds and jitter
Processing order can differ from arrival order unless you add more coordination
Hard to make deterministic

deepDives.choice: One pinned thread per partition, fed by a lock-free single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer. Numbers back it: the hottest symbol uses about 10% of a core at peak. Partitions are sized by measured load, and a very hot symbol can get a thread to itself. Code rules on that thread: no allocation, no system calls, no logging to disk, no reading the wall clock (time comes from the sequencer). If a single symbol ever exceeded one core, that is a sign the bottleneck is elsewhere; I'd first profile the per-message cost before splitting a book, which would break price-time priority.

deepDives.title: The sequencer and deterministic replay
deepDives.problem: Fairness, recovery and the standby all depend on one agreed order of inputs. If the primary and standby saw orders in different orders, their books would differ and failover would corrupt the market. We also must be able to rebuild any day's book exactly for audits and disputes.

options.name: Sequencer in front of the engine, journal of inputs
options.how: Every validated input gets a gap-free seq and timestamp. It is written to the journal and delivered to primary and standby. The engine is a pure function: same input sequence → same state and outputs.
pros: Standby is identical by construction, failover is instant
Recovery = load snapshot, replay journal after it
Audit replay reproduces any trade bit for bit
cons: The sequencer is on the critical path and must itself be highly available
Engine code must avoid every source of nondeterminism

options.name: Engine writes state changes to a replicated database
options.how: Primary applies orders and replicates resulting book changes.
pros: Standby does not need to rerun logic
cons: Much more data to replicate (every level change)
Database write on the hot path ruins latency
No exact replay of decisions

deepDives.choice: Sequencer plus input journal. The sequencer only acks to the engine once the standby (in the same datacenter, a few microseconds away) has the message in memory; the journal is flushed to NVMe in batches every few hundred microseconds and shipped to a second site. That gives no lost acked orders for a single-host failure without an fsync per message. Nondeterminism rules: time from seq stamps only, no iteration over hash maps in a meaningful order, no random numbers, same binary on both sides. A nightly job replays the full journal through a fresh engine and compares output hashes. If the business required zero loss through a full datacenter loss, I'd make the sequencer wait for the remote site and accept about a millisecond more latency.

diagram.title: Sequencing and failover
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant G as Gateway
  participant S as Sequencer
  participant P as Primary engine
  participant B as Standby engine
  G->>S: order clOrdId 77
  S->>S: stamp seq 9001 and time
  S->>B: seq 9001
  B-->>S: received
  S->>P: seq 9001
  P->>P: match, update book
  P-->>G: exec report for seq 9001
  B->>B: apply seq 9001, same result, output suppressed
  Note over P,B: primary dies, standby promoted, continues at seq 9002

deepDives.title: Market data fan-out
deepDives.problem: Hundreds of firms want every book change, and fairness means they should all get it at the same instant. At the open that is 800 Mbps of raw events; sending a separate TCP copy to each of 1 000 subscribers would need 800 Gbps and would deliver to the first socket before the last.

options.name: UDP multicast with sequence numbers, plus recovery services
options.how: Publisher sends each packet once to a multicast group per symbol range. Switches copy it. Each packet carries a channel seq. A subscriber that sees a gap asks a retransmit service, or rejoins from a periodic snapshot channel.
pros: Bandwidth independent of subscriber count
Everyone receives at nearly the same time
cons: UDP drops packets, so recovery logic is mandatory
Only works inside managed networks (colocation, private lines)

options.name: TCP per subscriber
options.how: Publisher keeps a socket per client and writes every event.
pros: Reliable, works over the internet
cons: Bandwidth scales with subscribers
A slow consumer creates backpressure and unfairness

options.name: Conflated WebSocket feed through edge servers
options.how: Downstream relays keep the current book and push a snapshot of top levels every 100 ms.
pros: Fine for apps and websites
Slow clients just miss intermediate states
cons: Not a full order-by-order feed
Too slow and lossy for trading firms

deepDives.choice: Two tiers. For members in the colocation facility: multicast order-by-order feeds sharded by symbol range, with gap fill from a retransmit service and a snapshot channel every second. Publish to two multicast groups over separate network paths (A and B feeds) so a single dropped packet rarely needs recovery. For everyone else: a conflated feed through ordinary WebSocket or REST servers that consume the multicast and serve depth-10 snapshots. Market data is generated from engine output after the matching thread, so publishing never slows matching.

deepDives.title: Latency budget and where tails come from
deepDives.problem: A median of 55 µs is easy to claim. The interview question is what makes the p99 or p99.9 jump to milliseconds, and how each hop is kept tight.

options.name: Kernel-bypass networking and pinned cores
options.how: Gateways, sequencer and engines use user-space network stacks and busy-poll. Threads are pinned to isolated cores so the OS never schedules anything else there.
pros: Removes interrupt and context-switch jitter, often tens of microseconds each
cons: Specialized hardware and ops skills
Busy cores burn power even when idle

options.name: Managed runtime with GC tuned or avoided
options.how: If written in a GC language, preallocate everything and avoid allocation on the hot path so collection never runs during trading. Otherwise use C++ or Rust.
pros: Team can still use a productive language for the rest of the system
cons: One accidental allocation in a hot loop brings back pauses

options.name: Durability without fsync per message
options.how: Replicate to a standby's memory before acking; flush to disk in batches.
pros: Removes a 10–100 µs disk write from every order
cons: Simultaneous loss of primary and standby can lose the last unflushed batch unless a remote copy is synchronous

deepDives.choice: The budget from the estimates: gateway 10, hop 5, sequence and replicate 20, hop 5, match 5, hop 5, send 5, total 55 µs. I'd do all three: kernel bypass on the gateway-sequencer-engine path, no allocation or GC on hot threads, and memory replication to a standby instead of fsync. All components sit in one datacenter, close together, because each extra switch adds microseconds. I'd measure with hardware timestamps on ingress and egress and alert on p99.9, not average. If the target relaxed to milliseconds (for example a crypto venue on cloud VMs), I'd drop kernel bypass and accept ordinary sockets.

failures: Lease-based controller promotes the identical standby in under 1 s. Gateways resume from the next seq; consumers dedupe outputs by seq.
Sequencer runs as a primary with a hot backup that sees every stamped message. Backup takes over at last seq + 1. Gateways resend unacked orders, deduped by clOrdId.
Detects the seq gap, requests retransmit for small gaps, or rejoins from the snapshot channel for large ones. A and B feeds make single drops rare.
Per-session message rate limits at the gateway, risk limits on open notional, and a kill switch that cancels all of a broker's orders.
Bug in a new engine release causes wrong fills
Shadow the new version on live input in parallel and compare outputs before cutover. The journal allows exact replay to find and correct affected trades.
Price collars and volatility halts: the engine pauses continuous matching for that symbol and restarts with an auction.
scale: More symbols: add partitions. Each is independent with its own sequencer and engine pair; gateways route by symbol.
Higher message rate: it is mostly cancels, so per-message cost matters most. Optimize the cancel path and add per-session rate limits and fees for excessive order-to-trade ratios.
More subscribers: no change for multicast. Add relay servers for the conflated tier.
Disaster recovery: ship the journal to a second site continuously. A cold site can rebuild books by replay in minutes; a warm one keeps engines replaying all day.

followups.q: Why not just use a database with row locks for the order book?
answer: A database round trip is 100 µs to milliseconds, already over the whole budget.
Locks give no guarantee that processing order equals arrival order.
We still get durability and audit from the journal, which is a better fit than a DB for an append-only input log.

followups.q: How do you keep the gateway risk check correct when fills happen in the engine?
answer: Gateway tracks open notional per broker from orders it sent and exec reports it receives.
It is a conservative running total: add on new order, subtract on cancel or fill.
Hard limits that must never be breached (for example credit) can be rechecked in the engine, at a small latency cost.

followups.q: How would you add an opening auction?
answer: Collect orders without matching. Publish an indicative price as orders arrive.
At the open time, choose the single price that maximizes matched volume, with tie-break rules.
Match all eligible orders at that price, then switch the symbol to continuous trading. It all goes through the same sequencer, so it is still replayable.

followups.q: How do you prove the system was fair to every broker?
answer: Sequencer timestamps and seqs show arrival order. The journal proves processing followed it.
Equal-length cables and the same gateway path for all colocated members, so no one is physically closer.
Market data via multicast reaches all members at the same time. Audit replay can reproduce any trade.

followups.q: What changes if this is a crypto exchange running in the cloud?
answer: Latency target becomes milliseconds; no kernel bypass or multicast in most clouds.
Keep the same core: sequencer, single-threaded engine, journal, standby replay.
Market data goes through WebSocket fan-out with conflation, and balances must be checked in the engine because there is no clearing house.

mistakes: Storing the order book in a database or cache and matching with queries.
Running matching on many threads with locks, then claiming price-time priority.
Forgetting cancels are most of the traffic and must be O(1).
Fanning out market data over per-client TCP without doing the bandwidth math.

mid: Explained price-time priority with a concrete fill example
Kept the order book in memory with a FIFO per price level
Separated order entry, matching and market data
Asked about order types and latency targets up front
senior: Used a hash map from order id for O(1) cancel and integer tick prices
Made matching single-threaded per partition and explained why it gives fairness
Added a sequencer and journal and showed how a standby stays identical
Computed market data bandwidth and chose multicast with gap recovery
Gave a latency budget per hop that adds up
staff: Listed concrete sources of nondeterminism and how replay is verified
Traded durability (sync remote copy) against latency and named when to pay it
Covered operational safety: kill switches, collars, shadow releases
Separated the colocated fast tier from a conflated public tier
